name: Marco Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What is an ordinary day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain the inspection-log software lift technicians use and trace faults from their signed sheet into the app; I like a record that tells the next technician exactly what happened. I don't use AI tools, and I am still learning the harder repair codes. My partner works part time at a bookshop, and our mortgage and two school-age children mean every paid hour matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a sorter can file the routine lift reports if it leaves the broken-door reports visible. I do not use AI tools; I read the technician's note and check the inspection date before changing our software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, my mid-level job should hold. I earn a normal developer wage, my partner works part time at a bookshop, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some software firms nearby. The mortgage fits our current wages, though the school costs leave little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing the inspection log and compare every door-fault report with the technician's signed sheet. In the first year we'd transfer 60 from my pay into a home-repair account only when the bookshop hours stay steady; I would not change the way I sign off faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the house budget, not about a small sorter. A broken washing machine would use most of what we have free this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a paper sheet show that the app missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A technician once wrote that a lift door stopped halfway, while the app showed the inspection as complete. I found the missing warning by reading the paper sheet against the digital record. The paper sheet showed a stopped lift door while the app called the inspection complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would the home-repair transfer stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bookshop hours dip after the school term begins. If that happens, we keep the 60 for groceries instead of moving it to a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing code, reading reports and answering building managers could reduce our team. I would ask management what happens to a stopped-door report before it replaces the person who checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the inspection logs, but the company might keep one senior developer and a tool instead of several of us. My three-month cushion would help with a search, yet part-time bookshop pay cannot carry the mortgage and children alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our manager for a list of checks a developer still signs and keep recording missed warnings from old reports. If the company pilots AI in the first year, I'd compare its output with technician sheets alongside a colleague who uses it; we'd postpone replacing the family sofa while staffing is unclear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can check the faults, but I would hate to be told the checker was the costly part of the process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What case would you insist on testing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stopped-door case belongs in any pilot. If the tool misses it, I want the error shown to the building manager, not filed as an odd exception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase could the family postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sofa is worn, but it still seats four. I would rather wait than turn a repair budget into furniture when the team may shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches inspection code and report checking before hands-on lift robots arrive around 2031. A broken door still needs a clear call to the people in the building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer post could go quickly when code and logs are cheap to process. Three months saved and some local firms give us a short search, but my partner's bookshop wage cannot cover the mortgage for four people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd put our mortgage dates and essential costs on paper and ask two lift firms about paid inspection-assistant places. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real openings with supervised hours whose wage plus my partner's reliable bookshop pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd search for other paid local jobs and ask the lender about hardship terms before a missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep calling firms. The code job that pays the house bill might vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a lift assistant role survive the later robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An inspection assistant must learn safety rules from a qualified technician before touching a lift. Robots may do more of that hands-on work around 2031, so I would ask firms whether trainees are actually paid beyond the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the family about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children we are keeping their school routine while I check the wages. I would not ask my partner to sell the house because a recruiter mentioned an opening that has no written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us see which inspection tasks still need a person at the lift. Robots arrive around 2034, but the thinking system changes our code before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the hands-on safety checks if an employer pays for an apprenticeship, though I might lose my software post first. Five years might let us grow savings if the bookshop hours hold; I would not pay for an expensive certificate without supervised work attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a lift technician to let me watch one inspection a month if my software manager releases the time. I'd start a paid apprenticeship only if supervision is real and the wage with my partner's dependable hours covers mortgage and school costs; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply only to actual paid openings that still meet those conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can ask about the work before leaving software. I would not call myself a technician after watching one inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you observe at the lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician would show me how a door fault is made safe before anyone resets the system. I'd stand clear until properly trained and authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask whether an apprenticeship is a full paid week or just a few days. We need written hours before we change the mortgage budget.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets us teach apprentices why a stopped door matters, not just how to press a button. Thinking AI reaches our code before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a paid lift-safety skill or still be writing software. Our three-month cushion and the bookshop's shorter weeks mean I cannot call today perfectly secure, though the extra time to prepare helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the door-fault log accurate and ask for more difficult inspection cases at work. We'd save 60 monthly only while bookshop hours allow, and in the first year after 2036 I'd switch to paid lift or software work only if a signed offer with my partner's dependable income covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about current bills, but less frightened by the distant date. A ten-year picture still starts with next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fault log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log would show the paper sheet, the missing warning and the correction, without a building resident's name. I want an employer to see how I found the mistake, not a copy of someone else's private report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your older child about apprenticeships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks about working with machines. I'd suggest a paid apprenticeship with a real supervisor if they enjoy that work, then let them decide when they know the costs and openings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because coding and report checks could disappear before I have a paid trade. A notice period, real lift-assistant vacancies with supervision, and a wage that meets our mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who is responsible when a warning disappears between the paper sheet and the app. The technician needs to know the door was faulty before anyone sends a lift back into service.

headlineQuote: The technician needs to know the door was faulty before anyone sends a lift back into service.
portrait: Marco, **43**, is an experienced lift-log developer with a bachelor's degree who checks digital faults against signed technician sheets.
His **typical pay**, partner's part-time bookshop hours and three-month cushion support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He avoids AI and remembers a **stopped-door warning** the app missed after a paper report.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about his post; 2028 AGI alarms him despite some nearby jobs.
With more time, he considers **paid lift training** only with supervision and wages covering household bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove software income before a paid, supervised lift role appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, real supervised vacancies and enough wages for the mortgage would help.
